source: He, Qiu, Sap, Shirado (2025) Martingale Score: an unsupervised metric for Bayesian rationality in LLM reasoning
finding: Gap 6. Tested whether LLM belief updates are predictable from the prior belief (a martingale violation, called belief entrenchment). Positive scores were nearly universal, also with reasoning (CoT) and debate. Entrenchment was worst in value-laden and paper-review domains and mildest in forecasting.
numbers: Models: GPT-4o, DeepSeek R1/V3, Gemini 2.0 Flash, Claude 3.5 Haiku, Llama 4 Scout/Maverick. 51 of 54 CoT setups had positive Martingale Score. Example CoT scores: GPT-4o forecasting +0.0018 (no prompt), +0.0156 (critical-thinking prompt); OpenReview about +0.07 to +0.10. For CoT forecasting a score of 0.0 gives Brier under 0.25; a score of 0.04 gives worse than chance.
quote: belief entrenchment is a pervasive phenomenon
limits: Beliefs are LLM-judge scored probabilities, not token probabilities. On OpenReview no link to accuracy was shown. Score is per reasoning step.
agent_relevance: An agent that rereads its own reasoning tends to lock on its first belief. Supports a rule: record a belief before and after evidence, and flag updates that only track the prior.

source: He et al. (2025) Martingale Score, model and technique comparisons
finding: Gap 6. Among seven models only DeepSeek R1 (a reasoning-trained model) showed significantly lower entrenchment, and its updates pointed toward ground truth more often. Debate reduced entrenchment; chain of thought did not. A prior-conforming prompt raised it and a critical-thinking prompt lowered it only in forecasting.
numbers: Other six models differed by small, non-significant amounts. Judge check: LLM judges correlate with the GPT-4o judge (for example DeepSeek-V3 0.7774, p<0.001). Entrenchment-accuracy link shown for forecasting only.
quote: DeepSeek R1 shows exceptional resistance to belief entrenchment
limits: One model is an n=1 outlier; the cause (RL on reasoning versus other training) is not isolated. Only 2025-era models.
agent_relevance: Reasoning traces alone do not make updating Bayesian-like. Structured opposition (debate, a second view) helps more than more thinking. Matches the schema idea of adversarial checking.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: evaluating and mitigating confirmation bias in language models
finding: Gap 9. Eleven LLMs played a Wason 2-4-6 style rule-discovery game, proposing their own test triples. They often chose tests that fit their current guess (confirmatory) and found the rule less often. Telling them to look for counterexamples helped.
numbers: Task success 6% to 78% across 11 models, max 45 turns. Success rose from 42% to 56% on average with human-derived interventions (Dual-Goal, Think-in-Opposites). Incompatible-to-compatible test ratio correlated positively with success, stronger for thinking models. Think-in-Opposites on Blicket test: Qwen3-32B success 0.57 to 0.86, ratio 0.54 to 1.31; Qwen3-8B 0.32 to 0.40.
quote: LLMs exhibit confirmation bias, often proposing triples to confirm their hypothesis
limits: Synthetic number rules (40 scenarios), one family of task. Thinking models gain without a consistent rise in the ratio, so gains are not only from less confirmation.
agent_relevance: Direct yes for gap 9: agent-generated disconfirming tests work, prompt-only, and the gain is large (14 points). Supports an operator that must propose a test the current hypothesis predicts will fail.

source: Jhaveri et al. (2026) Failing to Falsify, distillation results
finding: Gap 9. Fine-tuning on the traces produced under the falsification prompt moved behaviour into the weights and carried a smaller gain to the new Blicket task.
numbers: Qwen3-8B baseline task success 0.21, ratio 0.15; with Think-in-Opposites prompt 0.36, ratio 0.35 (10.88 to 7.37 turns). Wason-distilled students on Blicket improved over base but stayed below the prompt-based gain.
limits: Reported means; significance marks not all read. Student models only 8B and 32B.
agent_relevance: A scaffold gets most of the gain without training; training only partly matches it.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: uncertainty-aware planning enhances information seeking in LLMs
finding: Gap 10 and gap 1. UoT simulates answer branches, scores questions by information gain, and picks the best. At comparable token cost it beat self-consistency and a tree-of-thought baseline on 20 Questions, medical diagnosis and troubleshooting.
numbers: Table 2 (GPT-4 token use): CoT-SC k=33, 4.6k tokens: 20Q 32.6, diagnosis 37.6, troubleshooting 42.5. Adapted-ToT D=3, 4.5k: 33.8, 85.1, 60.3. Pruned UoT D=3, 4.7k: 48.1, 88.4, 63.2. UoT D=3, 9.2k: 54.4, 92.5, 66.0 (Adapted-ToT D=4 at 9.3k: 40.9, 86.7, 63.7). Average gain 38.1% success versus direct prompting; DX dataset 97.0% with GPT-4.
quote: UoT achieves an average performance improvement of 38.1%
limits: Baseline ToT is a sampling-based question generator, not plain diverse sampling. Answer simulation uses the LLM itself. Simulated patients in some sets.
agent_relevance: At equal tokens, information-gain selection beats vote-style sampling by about 10 to 15 points on 20Q and 3 to 8 on troubleshooting. Supports an EIG question-choosing operator.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts, reward ablation
finding: Gap 10. Removing the uncertainty (information-gain) reward lowered success but UoT without the reward still beat Adapted-ToT. So part of the gain is tree simulation, part is the reward.
numbers: Figure 4 (read from figure): ToT 33.8 vs ToT with uncertainty reward 45.3 on 20Q; UoT without reward 48.5 vs UoT 54.4 on 20Q.
limits: Figure-read values. Only the reward is ablated, not a diversity-only baseline.
agent_relevance: Information gain adds about 6 to 12 points on top of search alone in 20Q; effect is task dependent.

source: Mazzaccara, Testoni, Bernardi (2024) Learning to ask informative questions with preference optimization and expected information gain
finding: Gap 10. Sampled many questions from Llama 2 7B, scored each by expected information gain on 8 candidates, and trained with DPO on 55,000 high-EIG versus low-EIG pairs. This raised success and cut question count, partly out of domain.
numbers: Success@1 zero-shot to DPO: INLG 56.7% to 68.9%, Things 51.1% to 61.1% (gains +12.2 and +10 points), Celebrities 71.1% to 72.2%. Average questions fell by 2.1 to 2.3 on INLG and Things. With 16 candidates DPO +6.7 and with 29 candidates +13.8 points. Hypothesis-space EIG fell on BigBench (0.28 vs 0.31).
limits: Training method, not a scaffold. Closed candidate sets (polar questions). 7B model only.
agent_relevance: EIG as a filter of sampled questions is a cheap signal. Shows EIG separates good from bad samples, but the paper does not compare against plain diverse sampling.

source: Hutson et al. (2025) GuessingGame: measuring the informativeness of open-ended questions in LLMs
finding: Gap 10. In open-domain 20 Questions (858 games) a Bayesian information-gain score tracked efficiency. Simple prompt constraints that force question variety greatly raised success for Llama 3.3 70B. Human games matched the same pattern.
numbers: One SD more Bayesian IG cut expected game length by 43% (AFT coefficient -0.57, p=1.77e-7); entropy IG 19%. Success 39.4% default; 80.0% with a no-repeat-question-type constraint; 97.4% with forced open-ended questions; 32.1% binary-only. Humans: experts 96.3% success, 7.0 questions; naive 88.8%, 9.24 questions; Spearman -0.95 and -0.90.
quote: a one-standard-deviation IG increase reduces expected game length by 43%
limits: Small human sample (4 people, two were authors). Single model for interventions. IG measured by an LLM scorer.
agent_relevance: Simple diversity constraints can reach most of the gain without computing EIG, so diverse question sampling is a strong baseline. Not tested at matched tokens against EIG selection.

source: Lin, Dai et al. (2026, v2 Oct 2026) AdaptFuse: training-free sequential preference inference via externalized Bayesian computation
finding: Gap 1. Code holds the Bayesian posterior; the frozen LLM supplies likelihood-like signals via five samples. In the revised version the authors state the comparison is system-level, not equal-information, and that no symbolic-only baseline was run. Domains are still flights, hotels and web shopping.
numbers: Flight accuracy after round 5, Gemma 2 9B: self-consistency 44.7, Oracle Learning 59.1, Bayesian Teaching 73.4, AdaptFuse 76.2 (Llama 74.3 vs 76.3; Qwen 65.2 vs 67.3, teaching vs fusion). Without the positional EMA step the Gemma margin over Bayesian Teaching shrinks from 2.8 to 0.6 points. Cost per round: direct 0.52 s, CoT 2.15, self-consistency 3.67, AdaptFuse 4.35 s (5 LLM calls).
quote: much of the original margin depends on a temporal operation whose candidate alignment is not established
limits: Gain over self-consistency is large but over teaching small. Matched-token comparison absent. Parser, likelihood and hypothesis support were hand-built per domain. Table columns in the text extract were partly garbled; Gemma column checked against prose.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 stays open for diagnosis or rule discovery. The value of externalizing the posterior is likely real versus self-consistency but not shown versus a symbolic-only posterior.

source: Lin et al. (2026) AdaptFuse, sample budget and misspecification
finding: Gap 1 and 2. Accuracy rose with number of LLM samples N; three samples already nearly matched five. Wrong hypothesis grids cost a few points.
numbers: Flight Gemma: N=3 gives 72.8-73.3% at 2.63 s; N=5 exceeds the Bayesian Teaching point estimate. Hypothesis count M=24, 48, 96, 192 gives 71.8, 74.6, 76.2, 76.0%. Severe misspecification about 69.2 to 70.4%.
limits: Gemma, Flight task only for these sweeps. Not matched on tokens.
agent_relevance: Small sample counts (3 to 5) are enough when a code posterior aggregates them.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: scaling inference compute with repeated sampling
finding: Gap 2. Coverage (any sample correct) keeps rising with number of samples, but majority vote and reward-model picking plateau near 100 samples. Many samples help only when a verifier exists.
numbers: MATH, Llama-3-8B-Instruct: coverage 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000; majority vote or reward model only 40.50% to 41.41%. SWE-bench Lite, DeepSeek-Coder-V2: 15.9% with 1 sample to 56% with 250 (verified by tests).
quote: majority voting and reward models plateau beyond several hundred samples
limits: Math and code. Samples from one model share errors, which is why voting plateaus.
agent_relevance: Vul-style one-sample-per-person does not transfer: LLM samples are not independent. Aggregation helps up to tens of samples; beyond that, a checker is needed.

source: Kim, Garg, Peng, Garg (2025) Correlated errors in large language models
finding: Gap 2 (G4). Errors across different LLMs are strongly correlated; more accurate models make more similar errors. Even independent models are not independent voters.
numbers: Over 350 LLMs. On Helm (71 LLMs, 14,042 questions) model pairs agree about 60% of the time when both are wrong (a uniformly random wrong answer would give 1/3). HuggingFace leaderboard: 349 LLMs on 12,032 questions. Resume task: 20 LLMs, 1,800 pairs.
quote: models agree 60% of the time when both models err
limits: Multiple choice, across models, not repeated samples of one model (which are likely more correlated).
agent_relevance: The analogy to independent samples from a posterior breaks. Expect wrong answers to repeat, so voting cannot fix shared bias; use outside checks.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Are more LM calls all you need? Scaling properties of compound AI systems
finding: Gap 2. Majority vote over more calls first improves then can decline, because easy queries gain and hard queries lose when the model's modal answer is wrong. A model fitted to a few samples predicts the best number of calls.
numbers: Reported qualitatively in abstract and introduction; no single headline figure extracted this session.
quote: the performance of both Vote and Filter-Vote can first increase but then decrease
limits: Theory plus experiments on a few tasks; numeric details not read in full.
agent_relevance: More samples are not free gains. Use a small k and estimate it per task.

source: Wang et al. (2022) Self-consistency improves chain of thought reasoning
finding: Gap 2. Sampling many reasoning paths and voting beat greedy decoding; gains saturate quickly with path count.
numbers: Gains over greedy CoT: GSM8K +17.9, SVAMP +11.0, AQuA +12.2, StrategyQA +6.4, ARC-challenge +3.9 points. Up to 40 paths, 10 runs averaged.
quote: in most cases the performance saturates quickly
limits: 2022 models (PaLM, GPT-3, LaMDA). Gains were smaller on commonsense tasks.
agent_relevance: Equal-token cost is k times a single path; most of the gain is by 5 to 10 paths.

source: Qiu et al. (2025) Bayesian teaching enables probabilistic reasoning in LLMs, appendix D.1 LLM priors
finding: Gap 3. The authors audited the model's prior by asking it for verbalized beliefs before any interaction. Gemma 2 9B put most weight on no preference (except fewer stops); Gemini 1.5 Pro had a diffuse prior favouring cheaper, shorter, earlier flights.
numbers: Two models audited, flight features (departure, duration, stops, price). No accuracy gain from correcting the prior was tested.
limits: The authors warn verbalized priors may not match the prior the model uses when it acts. No correction experiment.
agent_relevance: Prior audit by asking is possible and cheap but unvalidated. Gap 3 half-closed: elicitation works as a diagnostic, benefit of correcting it is untested.

source: Qiu et al. (2025) Bayesian teaching, appendix on human users and prior typicality
finding: Gap 8. Untuned LLMs did better with real people than with uniformly sampled simulated users, because people prefer common things (cheaper flights). Restricting simulated users to human-like preferences lifted Gemma Original from 37% to about 60%.
numbers: 500 participants (10 per list, 50 lists), 5 rounds. Gemma Original about 60% on human-like reward functions versus 37% in the main figure.
limits: One task family. Typicality not varied as a continuous variable; no step that flags atypical users was tested.
agent_relevance: Accuracy depends on how typical the case is: the LLM leans on a common-case prior. A flag for atypical cases is plausible but untested (gap 8 measured, intervention open).

source: Qiu et al. (2025) Bayesian teaching, generalization experiments
finding: Gap 7. A model fine-tuned on flights transferred the skill to hotels (same structure) and to real web-shopping products, more than oracle teaching did. This is transfer of an updating skill, not of learned priors across problems.
numbers: Tasks: flight with 2 to 8 features, hotel (4 features), web shopping (10 users per category). Bayesian teaching beat oracle teaching on all; gap smaller on web shopping; remains below direct web-shopping fine-tuning.
limits: Weight-level transfer, not memory-based prior reuse by an agent. Exact accuracies are figure-only.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 stays open for in-context or memory priors. The cleanest evidence is about skills, not stored priors.

source: McCoy, Yao, Friedman, Hardy, Griffiths (2024) When a language model is optimized for reasoning, does it still show embers of autoregression? OpenAI o1
finding: Gaps 3 and 6. o1 beat earlier models, especially on rare task variants, but it still did better and used fewer thinking tokens when the output was high-probability text. Reasoning training softens but does not remove the prior's pull.
numbers: Quantitative tables not extracted this session; abstract states large gains on rare variants (for example acronyms from the second letter) and the same qualitative trend.
quote: optimizing a language model for reasoning can mitigate but might not fully overcome the language model's probability sensitivity
limits: Single reasoning model (o1, Oct 2024). Same research group as the original.
agent_relevance: Low-probability correct answers stay risky under reasoning; thinking length is itself a signal of low prior probability.
